validated_work_order.understanding: The register's Upcoming rows for a schedule come from `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` (packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.ts:517). It builds the schedule's occurrence dates, applies `dates.shift()` when `status === 'paid'`, and then filters the rest with `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` called once per occurrence over the WHOLE posted-transaction list. For the schedule kind a person creates by hand (`posts_transaction: false`, date condition `isapprox` — ScheduleEditModal.tsx:76, schedule-edit-utils.ts:49), `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate` returns `occurrenceDate - 2 days`, and the fallback arm accepts any transaction dated in `[occurrenceDate - 2, occurrenceDate]`. That window is an interval, so when occurrences are closer together than the lookback it overlaps several occurrences: a daily or every-other-day schedule gets one payment matched against three occurrences at once. `link-schedule` (server/rules/action.ts:235) never writes `schedule_occurrence`, so every rule-matched transaction on a synced budget is unstamped and takes that fallback arm. The same defect exists one more time over: when `status === 'paid'`, `dates.shift()` removes the head and then the fallback re-offers the very same transaction to the occurrence after it, which is why the reported symptom is three rows on a `due` schedule and four on a `paid` one. I reproduced both numbers.
validated_work_order.root_cause: The occurrence matcher is a per-occurrence predicate applied to an unbounded transaction list, so nothing stops one transaction from being counted for several occurrences. The overlap only bites when the gap between two occurrences is smaller than the 2-day lookback, which is why every shipped test missed it: `makeSchedule()` in schedules.test.ts uses `posts_transaction: true` and an `op: 'is'` date condition, both of which make `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate` return the exact occurrence date and collapse the window to a single day. The fallback arm was never exercised through `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions`.
validated_work_order.approach: Make the match one-to-one. Add `matchPostedScheduleOccurrences` to `packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.ts`: given a schedule, its schedule id, the occurrence dates under consideration and the schedule's posted transactions, it returns the `Set<string>` of occurrence dates that are discharged, and it guarantees each transaction discharges at most one occurrence. `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` calls it instead of filtering with `isScheduleOccurrencePosted`, and passes the coarse `status === 'paid'` claim as `paidByStatusDate` so that the transaction the status query matched is spent on the head and cannot also be handed to a later occurrence. The `dates.shift()` line stays exactly where it is — it is what drops the head when the posted-transaction list has not loaded yet, and it is what makes a payment dated AFTER the occurrence count as paid, which the two-sided comparison deliberately does not. Use the same matcher in the forecast, which repeats the same per-occurrence call over the same list and has the same defect. Worked example (verified by running the prototype): daily manual schedule, occurrences 2017-01-02..2017-01-31, one unstamped schedule-linked transaction dated 2017-01-05. Today 3 rows vanish (2017-01-05, -06, -07) when the status is `due`, and 4 when it is `paid` (the shift takes -02 as well). After the change exactly 1 row vanishes in both cases. Invariant for any input: the number of occurrences removed is never greater than the number of posted transactions carried for that schedule, and no occurrence is removed unless a distinct transaction can be named for it.

files.change:
Add an exported function immediately after `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` (currently ends at line 172), with this signature and no other new exports:

export function matchPostedScheduleOccurrences({ schedule, scheduleId, occurrenceDates, postedTransactions, paidByStatusDate }: { schedule: ScheduleOccurrenceMatchInput; scheduleId: string; occurrenceDates: readonly string[]; postedTransactions: PostedScheduleTransaction[]; paidByStatusDate?: string; }): Set<string>

Body, in this order:
1. `const ordered = [...occurrenceDates].sort();` — `yyyy-MM-dd` sorts lexicographically into chronological order.
2. `const paid = new Set<string>();`
3. Build `claimable`: `postedTransactions` mapped to `{ tx, index }`, filtered to `tx.schedule === scheduleId`, sorted by `tx.date` ascending and, for equal dates, by `index` ascending (Array.prototype.sort is stable, so an explicit index tie-break is belt-and-braces but keep it — the input order from `getPostedScheduleTransactionsQuery` has no ORDER BY).
4. If `paidByStatusDate` is set: find the FIRST entry of `claimable` whose `tx.schedule_occurrence === paidByStatusDate`, or whose `tx.schedule_occurrence == null` and `tx.date >= getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, paidByStatusDate)`. That entry is the one `getHasTransactionsQuery` matched to produce the coarse status bit; remove it from `claimable` and do nothing else with it. Do NOT add `paidByStatusDate` to `paid` — the caller's `dates.shift()` already removes that row, and adding it here would duplicate the mechanism. If no entry qualifies, remove nothing (this is the case where the posted-transaction list has not loaded yet, and the shift must still fire on its own).
5. Stamped pass: for each `occurrenceDate` of `ordered`, if any remaining entry of `claimable` has `tx.schedule_occurrence != null && tx.schedule_occurrence === occurrenceDate`, `paid.add(occurrenceDate)`. Two stamps naming the same occurrence still mark it once. A stamp naming a date outside `occurrenceDates` matches nothing.
6. Unstamped pass: for each remaining entry of `claimable` whose `tx.schedule_occurrence == null`, in the sorted order, find the FIRST `occurrenceDate` of `ordered` that is not already in `paid` and satisfies `tx.date >= getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, occurrenceDate) && tx.date <= occurrenceDate`; if one is found, `paid.add(occurrenceDate)`. Each entry is visited once, so it can claim at most one occurrence, and `paid` guards it from claiming one another entry already took. An unstamped transaction never claims an occurrence that a stamp took, and a stamped transaction never takes part in this pass.
7. Return `paid`.

In `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` (lines 594-604), replace the `const unpaidDates = dates.filter(date => !isScheduleOccurrencePosted({...}))` expression with:

  const paidDates = matchPostedScheduleOccurrences({
    schedule,
    scheduleId: schedule.id,
    occurrenceDates: dates,
    postedTransactions:
      postedTransactionsBySchedule.get(schedule.id) ?? [],
    paidByStatusDate: status === 'paid' ? schedule.next_date : undefined,
  });
  const unpaidDates = dates.filter(date => !paidDates.has(date));

Leave the `if (status === 'paid') { dates.shift(); }` line above it exactly where it is, and leave `forceUpcoming`, the sort and everything else in the function alone. Extend the comment block at lines 584-593 so it still explains why the two filters are not redundant, and adds: the shift spends the transaction the status query matched, which is why the matcher is handed `paidByStatusDate`, and the matcher is what stops that same transaction being offered to the occurrence after it. Do not change `isScheduleOccurrencePosted`, `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate`, `getHasTransactionsQuery` or `getPostedScheduleTransactionsQuery` — `getHasTransactionsQuery` in particular is load-bearing for `hasTransactionForSchedule` and `advanceSchedulesService`.
files.why: The fallback window is an interval, so the same predicate over the same list counts one payment once per occurrence it overlaps. Allocating transactions to occurrences is the fix the issue names; putting it in the shared module means the preview and the forecast cannot drift.

[] });` and replace the body of the `isScheduleOccurrencePosted({...})` guard in the `for (const date of occurrenceDates)` loop with `if (paidDates.has(date)) { continue; }`. Do not pass `paidByStatusDate` — the forecast never shifts its occurrence list, so there is no coarse claim to spend. files.why: This is the second caller of the same predicate over the same kind of list, and it has the identical defect: on a manual daily schedule one early payment makes the forecast omit the two following occurrences, understating the projected balance. Fixing only the preview path would knowingly leave it. It is called out in `risks` because it changes forecast balances, which no acceptance criterion on the issue covers.

cases: New fixture in the `per-occurrence preview filtering` describe: `makeManualRecurringSchedule({ frequency, every })` returning a `ScheduleEntity` with `posts_transaction: false` and `_conditions: [{ field: 'date', op: 'isapprox', value: { start: '2017-01-02', frequency, patterns: [] } }]`, plus a `DAILY_OCCURRENCES` list of the 30 dates 2017-01-02..2017-01-31 that `currentDay() === 2017-01-01` with a '30-day' window produces. This is the fixture the shipped suite never had: `makeSchedule()` uses `posts_transaction: true` and `op: 'is'`, so the shipped suite never reached the 2-day lookback.
A daily manual schedule with one unstamped schedule-linked transaction dated 2017-01-05 drops exactly one row (2017-01-05) out of the 30, for status 'due' and for status 'paid'.

The same for an every-other-day schedule (occurrences 2017-01-02, -04, -06, ...), payment on the head date with status 'paid', and payment on a later occurrence date with status 'paid' — exactly one row each.
Two unstamped transactions on a daily manual schedule drop exactly two rows, never three.
A sweep over every payment date in a daily schedule asserting the number of removed occurrences is at most 1 per transaction, for both 'due' and 'paid' status — the invariant the issue asks for.

A weekly manual recurring schedule (`isapprox`, `posts_transaction: false`) with one unstamped transaction dated two days before an occurrence still drops that occurrence and leaves the other three — the early-payment fallback keeps working (IAC-2).

A schedule whose date condition is `op: 'is'` and a schedule with `posts_transaction: true` on a daily cadence: an unstamped transaction drops only the occurrence whose date it carries, and one dated the day before drops none (IAC-3).
The head still drops when the status is 'paid' and the posted-transaction list is empty or contains nothing that can explain it — the `dates.shift()` path is not redundant with the matcher.

A direct `describe('matchPostedScheduleOccurrences')` block covering: a stamp credits its occurrence however the transaction is dated; a stamp naming a date outside the list matches nothing; a transaction for another schedule is ignored; unstamped transactions are matched to the earliest still-unpaid occurrence whose window contains them; `paidByStatusDate` spends the earliest transaction the status query could have matched and leaves the rest of the list available; with `paidByStatusDate` set but no matching transaction, nothing is spent and the returned set is empty.

Every existing case in this file must still pass unchanged — the weekly OCCURRENCES block at lines 483-682 and the `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` / `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate` / `getHasTransactionsQuery` blocks.

A manual recurring daily schedule (`op: 'isapprox'`, one occurrence per day, `posts_transaction: false`) with one unstamped schedule-linked transaction dated on the first occurrence: the forecast still carries an occurrence on the day after and on the day after that. Today the two following days are dropped as well, so this is the regression case for the forecast change.

The two existing `does not double-count schedule occurrences already posted on the due date` cases (monthly and the `op: 'is'` daily one) must still pass — their windows are a single day, so this change must not move them.

acceptance.check: On a schedule whose occurrences are one day apart, one schedule-linked transaction removes exactly one Upcoming row for that schedule in the register, and every other Upcoming row for that schedule is still listed.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Schedules -> Add schedule: a payee and amount used by nothing else, frequency 'Days', interval 1, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF. Open the register, count the Upcoming rows for that schedule. Add one transaction with that payee and amount dated on one of the occurrence dates; the schedule's rule links it (unstamped). The count must drop by exactly 1 — today it drops by 3, or by 4 if the schedule's badge reads Paid. Note WHICH row disappears: when the schedule's own next_date is the one the status query matched, the row that goes is next_date, not necessarily the row carrying the payment's date. Both are exactly one row; the criterion is the count, not which row. Do the same on an 'Every 2 days' schedule.

acceptance.check: An unstamped transaction dated up to two days before an occurrence still discharges that occurrence, so the early-payment fallback keeps working.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Schedules -> Add schedule: frequency 'Weeks', interval 1, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF, starting on a known Monday. Open the register and note the Upcoming rows. Add one transaction with that schedule's payee and amount dated the Saturday before the following Monday (two days early). The rule links it unstamped. Exactly the Monday row disappears; the other Mondays are untouched.

qa_script: Use 'View demo' on the setup screen for realistic data, then create the fixture schedule: Schedules -> Add schedule, frequency 'Days', interval 1, a payee used by nothing else, a distinctive amount, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF.
Go to the register and count the Upcoming rows carrying that payee. Record the count and the dates.
Add ONE transaction with that payee and amount dated on one of those Upcoming dates. The schedule's rule links it.
Count again. The difference must be exactly 1. Today it is 3.
Repeat with a second payment on a different occurrence date: the count must drop by exactly 1 again, cumulatively 2. It must never drop by 3 for one payment.
Repeat the whole sequence with frequency 'Every 2 days'. Same expectation.
Weekly schedule, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF: pay two days before an occurrence and confirm that occurrence's row goes and the other occurrences stay.
Weekly schedule with 'Post transactions automatically' ON: pay the day before an occurrence and confirm no Upcoming row moves.

Regression sweep: a weekly auto-post schedule with two payments for different occurrences still removes exactly those two rows, and an ordinary (non-recurring) schedule's single Upcoming row still disappears when it is paid.
Open the account's Reports -> Forecast with the daily schedule present and confirm the projected balance now includes the occurrences after the paid one.
risks: This narrows what counts as paid, on the path that decides which rows a user can still pay. The over-narrow direction is the dangerous one: a user who is behind and pays an occurrence dated AFTER `next_date` will now see that occurrence's row still offered, because the coarse `status === 'paid'` bit — which is by construction about `next_date` alone and is what `getHasTransactionsQuery` reports — claims that transaction for the head first. Today those rows all vanish (4); after the change 1 vanishes. The invariant 'one transaction discharges at most one occurrence' cannot hold together with 'a transaction dated after an occurrence still pays next_date' unless the transaction is attributed to `next_date`, which is what the plan does; the alternative, letting the matcher keep it, puts two rows back and fails IAC-1.

packages/loot-core/src/server/forecast/forecast-schedules.ts is changed too, and no acceptance criterion on the issue covers it. It changes forecast balances for budgets that have an unstamped schedule-linked transaction and occurrences less than 3 days apart: the forecast now includes occurrences it was silently dropping. That is a correction, but it is a visible change to a money number and it is a judgement call that the ticket did not ask for. It is listed here so a human can strike it before implementation.
The change is confined to `packages/loot-core/src/shared/`; nothing under `forbidden_paths` is touched, no dependency is added, and no host outside `env.api_allowlist` is contacted.

`getHasTransactionsQuery` is deliberately NOT touched. It is load-bearing for `hasTransactionForSchedule` and `advanceSchedulesService`, where widening it to later occurrences would make a later posted occurrence mark an earlier unpaid one paid. The two existing tests that pin that are at schedules.test.ts:381 and :412.
out_of_scope: Backfilling `schedule_occurrence` on transactions created by `link-schedule`. The narrowing above is what makes the unstamped path correct without it, and a migration is its own ticket.
`getHasTransactionsQuery`'s lower-bound-only fallback arm. It is deliberately wider than the two-sided comparison and the shift depends on it; changing it would move `next_date` for existing budgets.
The refresh tear the issue mentions (`useSchedules` publishing statuses and posted transactions independently, so rows can disappear for a round trip). Tracked in #41 and independent of this fix.

Advancing `next_date` past an occurrence the user has already paid. `advanceSchedulesService` owns that and reads `getHasTransactionsQuery`; changing it is a separate behaviour change on a different code path.

alternatives_considered.approach: Drop the multi-day lookback from the preview path entirely and leave early-payment matching to the status query alone, as the issue offers as an alternative.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It satisfies IAC-1 by making the fallback window a single day, but it breaks IAC-2 outright: an unstamped payment up to two days early would no longer discharge the occurrence it was for, and the register would re-offer an occurrence that was already paid. That is the double-payment direction the issue names as the risk of over-narrowing.

alternatives_considered.approach: Match occurrences to transactions (each occurrence takes the earliest eligible transaction) rather than each transaction to the earliest eligible occurrence.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It produces the same set of paid occurrences for every input I could construct, because the window `[occurrenceDate - 2, occurrenceDate]` is monotone in the occurrence date. The issue names the transaction-first direction, so that is what is specified; the implementer does not need to reason about the equivalence.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` and give it an extra parameter listing the occurrences already consumed.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A per-occurrence predicate given a shared mutable 'already consumed' list is how the two callers would have to be kept in step by hand, and it leaves the caller responsible for the ordering. A function that takes the whole occurrence list and returns the paid set makes the one-to-one rule impossible to get wrong at a call site.

alternatives_considered.approach: Fix the preview path only, and file the forecast as a follow-up.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The forecast repeats the identical per-occurrence call over the identical list and has the identical defect, and the fix belongs in the shared module anyway. Leaving one caller knowingly broken is the outcome the planner rules single out. Flagged in `risks` so a human can overrule.

assumptions: `dates[0] === schedule.next_date` in `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` — it is built as `const dates = [schedule.next_date]` and only ever appended to, so `paidByStatusDate` is always a date the caller's list has just shifted off.

`statuses.get(schedule.id) === 'paid'` means `getHasTransactionsQuery` matched this schedule, so the set of transactions that could have produced it is exactly `schedule_occurrence === next_date` OR `schedule_occurrence == null AND date >= getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, next_date)`. The plan replays that predicate in JS to pick the transaction the shift spends; the query itself is unchanged.

A QA user can reach the whole repro through the UI: the Schedules page's recurring picker offers 'Days', and a schedule created there writes an `isapprox` date condition with `posts_transaction: false`, which is exactly the shape that takes the fallback arm.
The register renders one Upcoming row per occurrence from `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions`, so the row count is the observable the acceptance criteria are written against.
unknowns: Whether a maintainer prefers the transaction the coarse status bit spends to be the EARLIEST that qualifies (specified here) or the one that falls inside the head's two-sided window (a later payment on a schedule the user is behind on would then be re-offered either way, but different rows survive). Both choices remove the same number of rows; only which row differs.
residual_risks: A user who is behind on a daily schedule and pays an occurrence dated after `next_date` sees that occurrence's row re-offered, because the status bit claims the transaction for `next_date`. That is the over-narrow direction, and it is inherent to keeping the shift while also guaranteeing one row per transaction. QA should exercise it and report what the register shows.

The change is a narrowing on a money path with no backfill: budgets whose unstamped transactions were being counted against several occurrences will see more rows return. That is the intended correction but it is visible.
validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: The defect was reproduced and measured (3 rows on a 'due' daily schedule, 4 on a 'paid' one), and the proposed design was run as a prototype against every assertion the shipped suite makes about weekly schedules, the two shapes the server test drives, and a 38-case sweep asserting one row per transaction. What remains uncertain is the tie-break inside the coarse status bit's claim, which changes which row survives and not how many.
